hallstatt.name: Hallstatt
hallstatt.summary: A small Austrian town known since prehistoric times for salt production, which gave its name to the Hallstatt archaeological culture.

urnfield-culture.name: Urnfield culture
urnfield-culture.summary: A late Bronze Age culture of Central Europe, roughly 1300–750 BC, named for its practice of burying cremated ashes in urns in fields.

amber-road.name: Amber Road
amber-road.summary: An ancient trade route carrying amber from the North Sea and Baltic coasts to the Mediterranean, later also used by the Roman Empire.

aquileia.name: Aquileia
aquileia.summary: Roman city near the Adriatic founded in 181 BC that grew to nearly 100,000 people, was sacked by Attila the Hun, and is now a UNESCO World Heritage archaeological site.

hallstatt-culture.name: Hallstatt culture
hallstatt-culture.summary: A Western and Central European archaeological culture spanning the Late Bronze Age through Early Iron Age (12th-6th centuries BC), commonly linked to Proto-Celtic peoples.

la-t-ne-culture.name: La Tène culture
la-t-ne-culture.summary: A European Iron Age culture that flourished from about 450 BC until the Roman conquest, spanning France, Central Europe and beyond, known for its swirling decorative metalwork style.

heuneburg.name: Heuneburg
heuneburg.summary: A prehistoric Celtic hillfort on the Danube in southern Germany, one of early Celtic Europe's most important centres and sometimes called the oldest city north of the Alps.

rhineland.name: Rhineland
rhineland.summary: A loosely defined industrial region of western Germany along the Rhine, with historic ties to the Holy Roman Empire, Prussia, and the German Empire.

publius-quinctilius-varus.name: Publius Quinctilius Varus
publius-quinctilius-varus.summary: A Roman general under Augustus whose loss of three legions to Germanic tribes led by Arminius at the Battle of the Teutoburg Forest in 9 AD ended Rome's expansion into Germania; he took his own life afterward.

kalkriese.name: Kalkriese
kalkriese.summary: A village in Lower Saxony, Germany, identified by archaeologists as the likely battle site, where more than 5,500 Roman military objects have been found since 1988.

augustus.name: Augustus
augustus.summary: Founder of the Roman Empire, ruling as its first emperor from 27 BC until his death in AD 14, and known earlier as Octavian.

germania.name: Germania
germania.summary: A historical region of north-central Europe in Roman times, stretching roughly from the Rhine to the Vistula, associated by Roman writers with the Germanic peoples.

arminius.name: Arminius
arminius.summary: Romano-German chieftain of the Cherusci (18/17 BC–AD 21) who commanded the Germanic alliance that destroyed three Roman legions at the Battle of the Teutoburg Forest in AD 9, halting Rome's expansion into Germania.

tiberius.name: Tiberius
tiberius.summary: Second Roman emperor, ruling from AD 14 to 37 as Augustus's stepson and successor, and earlier one of Rome's most successful generals.

germanicus.name: Germanicus
germanicus.summary: A Roman general and politician (15 BC to AD 19) known for his campaigns against Arminius in Germania; father of Caligula and grandfather of Nero.

germania-superior.name: Germania Superior
germania-superior.summary: A Roman province covering parts of today's western Switzerland, eastern France and southwestern Germany, with its capital at Mainz, made official around AD 85.

germania-inferior.name: Germania Inferior
germania-inferior.summary: A Roman province on the west bank of the Rhine, with its capital at modern Cologne, established around AD 85.

nero-claudius-drusus.name: Drusus the Elder
nero-claudius-drusus.summary: A Roman general and stepson of Emperor Augustus who led campaigns across the Rhine into Germania between 12 and 9 BC, dying after a riding accident that year.

lucius-domitius-ahenobarbus-consul-16-bc.name: Lucius Domitius Ahenobarbus
lucius-domitius-ahenobarbus-consul-16-bc.summary: Roman noble (49 BC–25 AD), son of a consul, who married the emperor Augustus's niece and became grandfather to emperor Nero through their son.

cherusci.name: Cherusci
cherusci.summary: A Germanic people who lived near the Weser River in what is now northern Germany, whose noble Arminius led the coalition that destroyed three Roman legions at the Teutoburg Forest in 9 AD.

negova.name: Negova
negova.summary: A Slovenian village, called Negau in German, near which the ancient bronze Negau helmets were discovered.

negau-helmets.name: Negau B helmet
negau-helmets.summary: One of 26 bronze helmets found near Negau, Slovenia, dating to about 450–350 BC; it bears a rare inscription in a northern Etruscan alphabet.

tacitus.name: Tacitus
tacitus.summary: A Roman historian and politician (c. 56–120 AD) whose works Annals and Histories chronicled the empire, regarded as one of Rome's greatest historians.

germania-book.name: Germania (book)
germania-book.summary: A work by the Roman historian Tacitus, written around 98 AD, describing the origins and customs of the Germanic peoples living outside the Roman Empire.

herodotus.name: Herodotus
herodotus.summary: Greek historian and geographer (c. 484–c. 425 BC), called 'the Father of History' for his Histories, a detailed account of the Greco-Persian Wars and the peoples and lands around them.

julius-caesar.name: Julius Caesar
julius-caesar.summary: Roman general and statesman, 100 to 44 BC, who became dictator of the Republic, expanded Roman territory through the Gallic Wars, and was assassinated in 44 BC.

elder-futhark.name: Elder Futhark
elder-futhark.summary: The oldest form of the runic alphabets, used by Germanic peoples from the 2nd to 8th centuries; its reading was forgotten until deciphered in 1865.

fenni.name: Fenni
fenni.summary: Ancient people first described by the Roman historian Tacitus in his 98 CE work Germania, living near the shores of the Baltic Sea.

grimm-s-law.name: Grimm's law
grimm-s-law.summary: Also called the First Germanic Consonant Shift, a set of sound laws describing how certain Proto-Indo-European stop consonants developed into Proto-Germanic, first discovered by Rasmus Rask and systematized by Jacob Grimm.

jeremy-j-smith.name: Jeremy J. Smith
jeremy-j-smith.summary: A British philologist and Professor of English Philology at the University of Glasgow.

lucian.name: Lucian
lucian.summary: Hellenized Syrian satirist and rhetorician (c. 125–after 180) known for tongue-in-cheek writings mocking philosophers and superstitions, written in Greek though his native language was probably Syriac.

liebenau-lower-saxony.name: Liebenau
liebenau-lower-saxony.summary: A small municipality in Lower Saxony, Germany, on the Weser river, where an early 5th-century runic inscription was found on a sword-belt disk.

aalen.name: Aalen
aalen.summary: A town in southeastern Baden-Württemberg, Germany, noted for its many half-timbered houses built from the 16th to 18th centuries.

meldorf-fibula.name: Meldorf inscription
meldorf-fibula.summary: A runic inscription on a first-century Germanic brooch found in Schleswig-Holstein in 1979, possibly the oldest known example of runic writing.

maroboduus.name: Maroboduus
maroboduus.summary: King of the Germanic Marcomanni (died AD 37) who, raised partly in Rome, led his people into Bohemia to escape Roman expansion and is the earliest recorded ruler of the modern Czech Republic's territory.

marcomanni.name: Marcomanni
marcomanni.summary: A Germanic people living along the Danube near the Roman frontier from about 60 BC to 400 AD, who formed a powerful confederation and later fought Rome in the Marcomannic Wars.

marcomannic-wars.name: Marcomannic Wars
marcomannic-wars.summary: A series of wars from about 166 to 180 CE between Rome and Germanic and Sarmatian peoples along the Danube, dominating the reign of Marcus Aurelius.

quadi.name: Quadi
quadi.summary: Germanic people with a kingdom centred in present-day western Slovakia from about 20 AD, prominent opponents of Rome during the Marcomannic Wars under Marcus Aurelius.

iazyges.name: Iazyges
iazyges.summary: A Sarmatian tribe that moved from Central Asia to the Ukrainian steppe around 200 BC, later settling near the Danube as a Roman client people who fought in Rome's Dacian and Marcomannic wars.

marcus-aurelius.name: Marcus Aurelius
marcus-aurelius.summary: Roman emperor from 161 to 180 and a Stoic philosopher, one of the 'Five Good Emperors' and the last emperor of the Pax Romana.

noricum.name: Noricum
noricum.summary: A kingdom or federation of tribes covering most of modern Austria and part of Slovenia, founded around 400 BC and made a Roman province in the first century AD.

illyria.name: Illyria
illyria.summary: A region of the western Balkans inhabited by the Illyrian tribes, whose borders and name shifted across Greek and Roman usage from antiquity into late Roman times.

catualda.name: Catualda
catualda.summary: A Marcomannic noble who returned from exile in 18 AD to depose King Maroboduus, before being defeated himself by Vibilius of the Hermunduri and settled by Rome in Gaul.

hermunduri.name: Hermunduri
hermunduri.summary: A Roman-era Germanic people known from written records between 7 BC and the 4th century, thought to have lived near present-day Bavaria and the Czech Republic.

vibilius.name: Vibilius
vibilius.summary: A 1st-century king of the Hermunduri, recorded by Tacitus for deposing the rival kings Catualda and Vannius among the Germanic tribes.

carnuntum.name: Carnuntum
carnuntum.summary: A Roman legionary fortress on the Danube that became capital of Pannonia Superior and grew into a city of about 50,000, near modern Vienna and Bratislava.

furtius.name: Furtius
furtius.summary: A 2nd-century ruler of the Quadi, a Germanic tribe, who negotiated a peace treaty with Marcus Aurelius but was deposed by his own people and replaced by Ariogaesus.

publius-silius-nerva.name: Publius Silius Nerva
publius-silius-nerva.summary: Roman senator and general under Augustus, consul in 20 BC alongside Marcus Appuleius.

gallienus.name: Gallienus
gallienus.summary: Roman emperor (c.218–268) who co-ruled with his father Valerian from 253 and alone from 260, fighting usurpers and Germanic invasions during the Crisis of the Third Century.

pannonia-superior.name: Pannonia Superior
pannonia-superior.summary: A Roman province created in 103 AD from the division of Pannonia, with its capital at Carnuntum; it covered parts of modern Hungary, Croatia, Austria, Slovakia and Slovenia.

aula-palatina.name: Aula Palatina
aula-palatina.summary: A Roman palace basilica in Trier, Germany, built around AD 300–310 and now used as a church; it holds the largest surviving hall from classical antiquity.

trier.name: Trier
trier.summary: A city on the Moselle in Germany, founded by the Romans in the late 1st century BC, considered Germany's oldest city and one of four imperial capitals during the Tetrarchy.

constantine-the-great.name: Constantine the Great
constantine-the-great.summary: Roman emperor from 306 to 337, the first to convert to Christianity, who legalized Christian worship across the empire and founded Constantinople as its new capital.

raetia.name: Raetia
raetia.summary: A Roman province named for the Rhaetian people, spanning parts of modern Switzerland, southern Germany and Austria, with its capital at Augusta Vindelicorum (Augsburg).

gallia-belgica.name: Gallia Belgica
gallia-belgica.summary: A Roman province covering what is now northern France, Belgium, and Luxembourg, created by Emperor Augustus in 22 BC after Caesar's conquest of Gaul.

proto-celtic-language.name: Proto-Celtic language
proto-celtic-language.summary: The reconstructed ancestral language of all Celtic languages, likely spoken between 1300 and 800 BC, associated with the Urnfield and Hallstatt cultures of central Europe.

germanic-paganism.name: Germanic paganism
germanic-paganism.summary: The traditional religion of the Germanic peoples, practiced for over a thousand years across Scandinavia, the British Isles and Germanic Europe, with belief in many gods and beings like giants and elves.

odin.name: Odin
odin.summary: A widely revered god of Norse mythology and Germanic paganism, associated with wisdom, poetry and frenzy, worshipped from Roman-era Germania through the Viking Age.

frigg.name: Frigg
frigg.summary: Goddess in Germanic and Norse mythology, wife of Odin, associated with marriage, prophecy and motherhood; the weekday Friday is named for her.

baldr.name: Baldr
baldr.summary: A god in Germanic mythology, son of Odin and Frigg; his death, recorded in Norse sources like the Poetic and Prose Eddas, was seen as a tragedy foreshadowing Ragnarök.

etruscan-civilization.name: Etruscans
etruscan-civilization.summary: A civilization of ancient Italy formed by a federation of city-states, with the earliest identifiably Etruscan culture dating from about 900 BC and its territory reaching its greatest extent around 500 BC.

golasecca-culture.name: Golasecca culture
golasecca-culture.summary: Late Bronze Age and Early Iron Age culture (9th–4th centuries BC) in northern Italy, named for its type-site near Golasecca and spread across a wide area south of the Alps.

ancient-celtic-religion.name: Celtic paganism
ancient-celtic-religion.summary: The polytheistic religion of the ancient Celtic peoples of Europe, worshipping gods such as Lugus and Taranis, with druids as priests and ceremonies held in sacred groves.

gallo-roman-culture.name: Gallo-Roman culture
gallo-roman-culture.summary: The blending of Gaulish and Roman culture, language, and customs in Roman Gaul, which persisted in parts of southern and central Gaul into the 7th century despite barbarian invasions.
